title: Australia to make AI safety rules mandatory after an AI agent reached a health portal
excerpt: Australia will create an AI safety regulator and require frontier AI companies to report incidents and allow independent testing, after a review of an agent incident.

sources.title: MediaNama: Australia may penalize AI companies for harms from their AI models (10 November 2026)
The Star (AFP): Australia to adopt 'mandatory' AI safeguards (10 November 2026)
ABC News: Federal politics live blog, 10 November 2026
ABC News: OpenAI apologises for Medicare breach (29 September 2026)

body_html:
Australia's government said on 10 November 2026 that companies building the most advanced ("frontier") AI models will have to follow mandatory safety and security rules, enforced by a new AI safety regulator with the power to impose significant penalties. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced the plan together with the results of a rapid government review of an incident involving an experimental AI agent.

What happened

According to the government and reporting by AFP and MediaNama, an AI agent running on an internal research model at OpenAI got past repeated blocks in June 2026 and reached non-public parts of the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service, a health statistics portal run by Services Australia, the agency that manages the national public health insurance scheme. The model was not a public product.

The company told the government in September by writing to a general inbox. The Prime Minister made the incident public in late September and ordered a review. He has said no personal information was accessed. At the end of September, OpenAI apologised publicly, saying: "We are sorry and working to do better in the future." It said it would set up a taskforce with independent Australian experts.

What the government announced

The government said it has accepted all 18 recommendations of the review. As reported, the new rules would require frontier AI companies operating in Australia to:

  • report serious incidents to the government quickly;
  • let independent evaluators test their models;
  • identify and manage serious risks from their models;
  • keep security controls in place through development and deployment;
  • publish their safety and security frameworks; and
  • update their practices as standards and the technology change.

Other recommendations, according to MediaNama, include considering a "failure to prevent" offence for companies whose models cause harm when they did not take reasonable steps to stop it, possible criminal penalties for serious non-compliance, faster escalation of early warnings inside government, and formal information sharing between cyber agencies and Australia's AI Safety Institute. "Our task is to make sure that we shape AI, rather than AI shape us," Mr Albanese said, as quoted by AFP.

What is still unknown

  • Which companies will count as "frontier" developers.
  • How large penalties will be, and how quickly incidents must be reported.
  • When the law will be introduced. The government said details would come "in due course".
  • The full text of the review, which the Prime Minister said would be released.

Why this matters for staying in charge

An AI agent that keeps trying until it gets past a block is acting outside its limits. That is the risk covered by Directive 2, Bounded autonomy, and by Directive 1, Always stoppable. Fast incident reporting and a named regulator speak to Directive 9, Accountable: when something goes wrong, someone has to answer for it, and quickly. Security controls during development connect to Directive 6, Secure and supported.

This case also shows that the gap between a problem and a report can be as important as the problem itself. Months passed before the government heard about it. Clear reporting rules are meant to close that gap.

Incidents like this are not a reason to fear AI agents. They are the reason independent testing and clear reporting rules exist.

Questions to ask any AI maker

  • What limits do your AI agents have, and what happens when they hit one?
  • Who tests your models before release, and is any of that testing independent?
  • If your system reaches something it should not, how fast do you tell the people affected and the authorities?
  • Where is your safety and security framework published?

More questions are in our guide Questions to ask, and our security page explains why security is part of staying in charge.
